tagline: Horse ranches and lakeside villages share a loop from Lake George
intro: The Dude Ranch Trail makes a 40-mile circuit from Lake George village through the southeastern Adirondack Mountains. Horse ranches, lakeside resort villages and theme parks line the loop. New York’s scenic-byway program identifies scenic and recreational qualities as its attractions, describing roads through Adirondack hamlets and past resorts and ranches.

Tourism had already reshaped travel at Lake George by the late nineteenth century. Railroad tracks extended onto the docks at the lake’s southern end, where steamboats departed several times daily for hotels farther north. The ranch-resort identity took hold in the 1920s, when Earl Woodward introduced dude-ranch-style resorts to the Lake George region. One later property, Hidden Valley Dude Ranch, began in 1939; Charles R. Wood and Paul Newman bought it at auction in 1991. They adapted its existing buildings for a medically safe children’s camp, Double H Ranch, which opened in 1993.

For a circuit through the river towns, take the Lake Luzerne leg first: NY 9N connects Lake George with Lake Luzerne, 11 miles to the southwest. Hadley lies across the Hudson, where the Sacandaga joins it. Continue the loop through Stony Creek and Warrensburg, on the Schroon River, before returning to Lake George.

moments.title: Hadley
moments.text: The Hadley Bow Bridge carries Corinth Road over the Sacandaga just above its meeting with the Hudson. Its long span has curved structural members above and below the roadway, placing the deck midway between them. Completed in 1885, it later faced demolition after deterioration and closures. Local preservation groups pressed to save it, and a restoration funded by federal and state grants brought a reopening in 2006. The ironwork spans a deep gorge whose sides rise steeply toward the road. Its stone abutments came from the bridge it replaced, built in 1813.
moments.notice: The bridge’s curved structural members arch above and below the roadway.

moments.title: Stony Creek
moments.text: Roaring Branch and Stony Creek meet near the former tannery site at the center of town. Stony Creek became a separate town in 1852, formed from the part of Warrensburg called Athol. During the tannery years, in the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries, the population reached 1,250 and logging extended across western Stony Creek. After many hemlocks were cut and tanning practices changed, the tannery closed and the population fell. The town’s business and social center is the four corners, where roads from Hadley and Warrensburg meet. A small park beside Roaring Branch occupies one corner.

moments.title: Lake George
moments.text: The fort in Lake George village is a reconstruction of Fort William Henry, replacing the original burned during the French and Indian War. The village, once called Caldwell, stood on the route between British and French colonies and saw military traffic during the colonial wars. By the last quarter of the nineteenth century, tourism was growing. Railroad tracks reached the steamboat docks at the lake’s southern end, where boats carried passengers north to hotels several times daily. The former railway station survives among the village’s historic sites, alongside a nineteenth-century courthouse and jail used as a museum.
